title: Pronunciation
subtitle: How Swiss German sounds
description: Learn the sounds of your dialect and discover how to pronounce words naturally.

expectations.title: Hear and recognise Swiss German sounds

sections.title: Vowels
sections.description: A, E, I, O, U and the special vowels Ä, Ö and Ü.

rules.title: A, E, I, O, U
rules.theory: Learn how the five basic vowels are pronounced in your dialect.
rules.note: Listen to each recording and repeat.
rules.takeaway: Compare the sounds with a language you know. I is similar to the vowel in English “see”, French “si” or Spanish “sí”. U is similar to the vowel in English “boot” or Spanish “tú”. These are guides: follow the audio.

rules.title: Ä
rules.theory: The letter Ä often has a sound similar to the vowel in the English word “bed”. It is different from a regular A sound.
rules.takeaway: Ä is an open front vowel. “Bed” in many English accents is a good starting point; the vowel in French “mère” may be closer. Listen to the recording.

rules.title: Ö
rules.theory: Learn how to pronounce Ö. This sound has no exact equivalent in most English accents.
rules.takeaway: Round your lips as if saying “oh”, but keep your tongue where it is for “eh”. The French vowel in “peu” or “deux” is a useful comparison.

rules.title: Ü
rules.theory: Ü is a rounded vowel sound that is unfamiliar to most English speakers.
rules.takeaway: Say “ee” while rounding your lips as if saying “oo”. The French U in “tu” is a particularly useful comparison.

rules.title: Short and long vowels
rules.theory: Some vowels are pronounced briefly, while others are held for longer.
rules.note: Compare “ofe” with “offe” to hear the difference, and listen to the long vowel in “Maa”.
rules.takeaway: Listen for how long the vowel is held. The spelling often shows it, and the audio is the reference for the exact sound.

sections.title: Consonants
sections.description: Sounds such as CH, SCH and R.

rules.title: CH
rules.theory: CH is one of the distinctive sounds of Swiss German. It is not pronounced like “ch” in “cheese”.
rules.note: The Scottish “loch” is a good reference for the throaty CH. The French R and the Spanish J (as in “jamón”) may help too, but they vary by speaker and aren't exact equivalents.
rules.takeaway: Make the sound with friction at the back of your mouth. Start with the CH in Scottish “loch”, then listen carefully.

rules.title: SCH
rules.theory: Learn how to pronounce SCH, a sound similar to “sh” in English “ship”.
rules.note: SCH is similar to “sh” in English “ship” and “ch” in French “chat”.
rules.takeaway: Keep the sound smooth and continuous, then match the audio.
